title: Rahul Gandhi Vows Campaign Against E20 Fuel as Consumer Backlash Intensifies
excerpt: The Congress leader accused the government of 'stealing money and destroying lives' through mandatory ethanol blending, joining a growing chorus of opposition from transport unions, social media movements and automakers.
body:
• Rahul Gandhi has pledged a sustained Congress-led campaign against India's mandatory E20 ethanol-blended fuel policy, accusing the government of damaging vehicles and wallets.
  • The backlash now spans opposition parties, transport unions, social media movements like the 'E20 Janta Party,' and the auto industry lobby SIAM, which flagged fuel contamination concerns.
  • The government has defended E20 as safe and clean, dismissing concerns as a 'misinformation campaign,' while the petroleum minister has ruled out offering unblended alternatives.
  • India's auto industry body withdrew its formal warning about chloride and moisture contamination in E20 fuel hours after it became public, citing the need to 'authenticate' the data.

Gandhi Escalates Opposition Attack on Fuel Policy

Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, has vowed to lead a sustained campaign against the central government's E20 ethanol-blended petrol policy, calling it a programme that is 'stealing money from people and destroying their lives.'

https://youtube.com/watch?v=FMrWWbYppoQ

The Congress leader's intervention marks the most prominent political escalation yet in a controversy that has roiled India for months, drawing in transport unions, consumer rights groups, social media movements and, briefly, the country's own automobile industry.

E20 petrol — a blend of 20 per cent ethanol and 80 per cent conventional petrol — replaced E10 nationwide at roughly 90,000 fuel stations in 2025, well ahead of an original 2030 deadline. The accelerated rollout was part of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's strategy to cut India's costly petroleum imports. But vehicles compliant with the new blend only started reaching showrooms in 2023, leaving millions of older cars and two-wheelers running on fuel they were not designed for.

Consumer Anger Finds Multiple Outlets

The E20 backlash has become India's first major consumer rights movement driven substantially by social media. An online movement calling itself the 'E20 Janta Party,' inspired by the earlier Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests, has attracted more than 2.95 lakh followers across X and Instagram. It demands consumer choice — the option to buy unblended petrol alongside E20 — rather than an outright ban on ethanol blending.

AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal launched a parallel online signature campaign through StopE20petrol.com, urging citizens to petition the Prime Minister for conventional petrol, E10 and E20 to be offered side by side at fuel stations. Kejriwal said party workers had spoken with motorists at fuel stations and service centres who reported reduced mileage, engine problems and higher maintenance costs.

Transport unions have taken the fight offline. The Delhi Taxi and Tourist Transporters and Tour Operators Association, the All India Motor Transport Congress, and the All India Motor & Goods Transport Association marched to Parliament on August 4 demanding the withdrawal of mandatory blending.

"We do not want to make this a political issue. This is damaging vehicles — we hope the government makes E20 blended petrol a choice for commuters."

— Rajender Kapoor, President, All India Motor & Goods Transport Association

Youth Congress Targets Gadkari

The Indian Youth Congress has staged street protests in Delhi targeting Union Minister Nitin Gadkari, a key proponent of the ethanol blending programme. Protesters wore Gadkari masks, distributed mock currency notes and set up live sugarcane juice machines to lampoon the government's ties to the sugar and ethanol industry.

Congress has alleged conflicts of interest involving Gadkari family-linked ethanol businesses, though the party's own complex relationship with the sugar cooperative sector — Sharad Pawar's NCP was a long-time Congress ally — has invited accusations of selective outrage.

Auto Industry's Warning and Quick Retreat

The controversy reached a new level when the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM), whose members include Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors, Toyota and Mercedes-Benz, sent a letter to the petroleum ministry on July 28 warning of elevated chloride and moisture levels in E20 fuel at retail outlets.

'Members are observing a huge increase in the issues in customer vehicle parts and replacement,' the letter, seen by Reuters, stated. 'Investigations reveal the failure is due to corrosion or wear caused by high chloride presence which is traced to the fuel used.'

But the warning lasted barely 24 hours in the public domain. After media reports triggered uproar, SIAM withdrew its communication on August 5, saying the numbers 'need authentication through collection of elaborate data across the country.'

Vehicle owners were unconvinced. 'Did the science change overnight, or did the ministry call?' Nachiket Deshpande, a user on X, asked — a sentiment echoed by thousands.

Government Holds Firm

The central government has shown no inclination to retreat. Petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri has ruled out offering unblended or E10 petrol alongside E20, citing logistical challenges involving separate storage, transportation and dispensing infrastructure. Minister of State Suresh Gopi told Parliament that the government had not received 'widespread or substantiated' complaints linking E20 to vehicle-performance issues.

A senior government official, speaking to Reuters on condition of anonymity, called the fuel concerns a 'misinformation campaign' playing out mainly on social media with 'no real evidence in cars on the road.' The government has pointed to its own data showing only two cases of chloride contamination in a sample of 2,000 tests.

Meanwhile, the Automotive Research Association of India has been tasked with examining whether blending could be increased further to E25 — a prospect that has done little to reassure sceptical motorists.

What Comes Next

Gandhi's promise of a sustained campaign signals that E20 will remain a political battleground through the year. With Parliament in session, opposition parties are expected to press for a formal debate on the policy. For Indian consumers — and the roughly 250 million vehicle owners affected — the core demand remains straightforward: give us a choice at the pump.
